summary: For ages 7-9: teach three insect anti-predator strategies — camouflage (hiding by blending in), warning colours (bright patterns advertising 'I'm dangerous'), and mimicry (a harmless insect copying a dangerous one). The unifying idea is FUNCTION: each strategy helps an insect avoid being eaten, but by different logic (hide vs. advertise vs. impersonate). Frame everything from the predator's point of view — why does each trick work on the eater? Treat it as observed phenomenon here; the natural-selection mechanism comes later (ages 9-11).
misconceptions: 'Camouflage means the insect chooses/decides to hide' — it's a fixed appearance, not a deliberate act.
'Bright colours are just for looking pretty' — warning colours function to deter predators.
'A mimic is actually dangerous' — the whole point is it's harmless but LOOKS dangerous.
'Predators are stupid to be fooled' — the tricks exploit sensible predator learning/avoidance.
Confusing warning colours (real danger, advertised) with mimicry (fake danger, borrowed).

activities.title: Play the hungry bird: feeling why each trick works
steps: Take the role of a hungry bird hunting bugs across leafy, twiggy backgrounds; tap prey to 'eat' them.

Notice that camouflaged insects are genuinely hard to find — a 'twig' turns out to be a stick insect, a 'leaf' turns out to be a leaf insect — so the hidden ones survive because you (the predator) can't spot them.
Eat a bold black-and-yellow caterpillar and receive a 'yuck' penalty; next time that bright pattern appears, decide whether to leave it.
When a harmless hoverfly appears wearing wasp stripes, decide whether to eat or avoid it, then reveal that it was a harmless bluff.
Afterwards, state in your own words how camouflage, warning colours, and mimicry each led to 'not eaten'.
activities.insight: Experiencing all three tricks from the eater's side: camouflage hides, warning colours teach the predator a lesson, and mimicry borrows someone else's scary reputation — all so the insect does not get eaten.

activities.title: Spot it and reveal it: a 'can you spot it?' habitat scene
steps: Search a busy habitat picture to find hidden stick and leaf insects; tap or point to reveal each one.
For bright-coloured bugs, open a callout explaining what the colour is telling predators.
For a wasp-and-hoverfly pairing, identify which look-alike is the harmless mimic and which is the real danger.
Count how many camouflaged insects you missed on the first pass to feel how well hiding works.

Predict what would happen to a green leaf insect placed on bare brown soil instead of green leaves — would it still be hidden? — and explain why matching the background matters for camouflage to work.
activities.insight: Recognising the three categories first-hand: camouflaged insects are hard to find, warning colours are a message, and a mimic can look very similar to its model — and seeing that camouflage only works when the insect's appearance matches its surroundings, so it can fail on the wrong background.

activities.title: Sort and explain the strategies
steps: Sort a set of insects into three groups: camouflage, warning colours, and mimicry.
Match each mimic to the dangerous model it copies (hoverfly to wasp).
Answer: 'Why do a wasp's bright stripes help it survive?' and justify your choice.
Explain in a sentence why a harmless hoverfly with wasp stripes is still left alone by predators.
activities.insight: The three strategies are distinguished by their logic, and warning colours work because a predator often learns to avoid that pattern after a bad experience with it.

activities.title: Ask the bird (optional dialogue)
steps: Interview a bird character: 'Why don't you eat the stripy ones?' and 'Why did you leave the hoverfly alone?'
Press further: 'What happened the first time you tried to eat something stripy?' to surface the learned-avoidance logic.
Use the bird's answers to write or say why each strategy keeps an insect from being eaten.
activities.insight: Putting the predator's reasoning into words — avoidance often follows a bad experience, and a convincing copy earns the same avoidance.

checkQuestion: A wasp has bright yellow-and-black stripes that are easy to spot, but a stick insect is hard to see because it looks just like a twig. Both of these help the insect stay alive — how? And a harmless hoverfly ALSO has yellow-and-black stripes even though it has no sting. Why would that help it?
checkAnswer: The stick insect uses camouflage — blending in so predators can't spot it to eat it. The wasp's bright stripes are a warning: they tell predators 'I can sting — leave me alone', so predators learn to avoid it. The harmless hoverfly uses mimicry — it copies the wasp's warning colours, so predators avoid it too even though it can't actually sting; it gets the protection without the sting.
